SOURCE: "Towards AI Search Paradigm", Yuchen Li, Hengyi Cai, ... Shuaiqiang Wang, Dawei Yin (Baidu Search; corresponding author Yin). arXiv:2506.17188v2 [cs.CL], 13 Mar 2026. Preprint, no venue printed. The first-author surname is Li, so the file name li-2025 fits (v1 was June 2025).

COVERAGE: 213,672 chars total. I read chars 0-175,020 in full (abstract through conclusion, all of Sections 1-8, all equations and table captions). The remaining ~38k chars are references. I skimmed them only by regex lookup of the origins named below. Extraction is clean text. I did not run the figures script; figure captions come from the extracted text.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. The paradigm is four LLM agents (Master, Planner, Executor, Writer), and the Master picks one of three team configurations by query complexity.
   - number: none (3 configurations)
   - setup: a design blueprint at Baidu Search. No ablation compares the three configurations or compares teams against a single agent.
   - quote: "the AI search system adopts three distinct team configurations to support different levels of reasoning and execution: (1) Writer-Only Configuration, (2) Executor-Inclusive Configuration, and (3) Planner-Enhanced Configuration."
   - where: Sec 2, ~char 8,500 (p.8)
   - Master role: "analyzing the user's input query to assess its complexity and intent, and for assembling an appropriate team of specialized agents ... without directly participating in the downstream query processing itself."
   - Planner is "only invoked for complex queries".
2. The Planner emits the whole DAG in one pass, and the Executor runs it layer by layer.
   - number: none
   - setup: the planner receives the query q plus a candidate tool set T, and produces G=(V,E). Each node is an atomic sub-task with at most one tool type bound, though the tool may be called several times. The prompting strategy is chain-of-thought then structured JSON sketch.
   - quote: "Unlike iterative ReAct-style reasoning, this approach produces a machine-readable, verifiable global plan simultaneously, substantially reducing token consumption and simplifying downstream parsing."
   - quote: "schedules execution by topological depth ℓ(·). For each layer V_d = {v | ℓ(v)=d}, all vertices are carried out in parallel."
   - where: Sec 3.4, ~char 62,000 (p.18-19)
   - Node interface is <arg(v), ret(v)>; ret(v_i) is propagated along edge (v_i, v_j) to fill arg(v_j). The paper's own claim is that the DAG gives "minimal context length, layer-wise parallelism, and full traceability." These are asserted, not measured.
3. Failure handling is local. The Master relays the failure to the Planner, which rolls back and re-plans only the affected subgraph. The Master also adds downstream nodes when results are incomplete.
   - number: none
   - setup: described only, with no failure-rate or cost data.
   - quote: "the Planner initiates a localized rollback and re-planning on the affected subgraph while preserving the remainder of the DAG G. This method enhances robustness without incurring the cost of a global restart."
   - quote (Sec 3.5): "If the results are found to be incomplete, the Master guides the Planner to augment the existing DAG by incorporating additional downstream sub-task nodes"
   - where: Sec 3.4-3.5, ~chars 62,500-64,000
4. Executor-level fallback: if a tool fails, the Executor switches to a functionally equivalent tool in the same k-means++ cluster ("toolkit") of LLM-described tools. The Executor also loops tool calls until it judges the output sufficient.
   - number: none (k is a free parameter)
   - where: Sec 2 and Sec 3.3.2, ~chars 11,500 and 50,000
5. Dynamic capability boundary: tool retrieval narrows the tool set to about a dozen before planning.
   - number: ~12 tools
   - setup: Baidu's experience, not an experiment.
   - quote: "the dynamic boundary typically consists of a relatively small set of tools, around a dozen tools, which proves sufficient to carry out task planning."
   - where: Sec 3.3, ~char 41,000
   - Retrieval is an LLM dual-tower retriever plus COLT (Qu et al. 2024), which models tool collaboration through query/scene/tool bipartite graphs so the retrieved set is complete.
6. Planner RL: GRPO with a rule-based reward summed from four parts (final answer, user feedback, format, intermediate execution).
   - number: none (the alphas and betas are unspecified)
   - quote: "R_All = R_Answer + R_Feedback + R_Format + R_Execution" (Eq. 15)
   - quote: "optimizing the Planner in isolation may prove insufficient and could lead to suboptimal performance of the overall system."
   - where: Sec 3.6, ~char 65,000
   - No planner RL results are reported.
7. Joint multi-agent training (MMOA-RAG, Chen et al. 2025b) trains the Planner (query rewriter), Executor (document selector) and Writer with MAPPO and a shared F1 reward.
   - number: planner penalty -0.5 if more than 4 sub-questions; selector penalty -1 for invalid IDs; writer penalty -0.5 if over the length limit
   - setup: the three agents share one LLM backbone, the web search tool is treated as environment, and there is an SFT warm start. This is the paper's cited method, not a result of this paper.
   - quote: "P_QR = −0.5 when the number of sub-questions exceeds 4, and is 0 otherwise."
   - where: Sec 5.5, ~chars 117,000-122,000
8. Headline evaluation: human side-by-side against Baidu's legacy web search shows no gain on simple queries and a significant gain on complex ones.
   - number: NWR 0.00% simple, +5.00% moderately complex, +13.00% complex
   - setup: Baidu Search, professional blind annotators, real user queries. DeepSeek-R1 classified query complexity (targeted sampling). The metric is NWR=(#Win−#Lose)/(#Win+#Tie+#Lose). t-test p<0.05 on the two non-zero cells. The sample size is not stated. The comparison is whole system vs legacy search engine.
   - quote: "AI Search 0.00% 5.00%∗ 13.00%∗" (Table 1)
   - where: Sec 7.1, ~char 150,500 (p.49)
9. Online A/B test: small engagement gains.
   - number: CQR -1.45%, PV +1.04%, DAU +1.85%, dwell time +0.52%
   - setup: 1.00% of Baidu Search traffic, relative to the legacy system, all p<0.05.
   - quote: "the change query rate (CQR) decreases by 1.45%; the number of page views (PV) increases by 1.04%; the number of daily active users (DAU) increases by 1.85%; dwell time (Dwell Time) increases by 0.52%."
   - where: Sec 7.2, ~char 153,000 (p.50)
10. Qualitative case: the same query "Who is elder, Emperor Han-Wu or Emperor Caesar, by how many years?" is used throughout. Vanilla RAG returns the wrong person, and ReAct and RQ-RAG are argued unable to compute the difference without a calculator tool. The argument is by example, with no benchmark.
   - number: none
   - quote: "ReAct's reliance solely on in-context memory precludes genuine external tool invocation"
   - where: Sec 3.1, ~chars 29,500-33,000
   - Planner DAG for the example: Sub-Task 1 (Web Search, Han-Wu birthdate), Sub-Task 2 (Web Search, Caesar birthdate), Sub-Task 3 (Programmer tool, difference). Tasks 1 and 2 run in parallel (Sec 7.3).
   - The paper's own sample answer says Han-Wu "older by approximately 56 years", and the Fig. 15 text says "56 years older than Caesar" (born 156 vs 100 BCE).

Other numbers in the paper (peripheral to topology):
- Inference section: DeepSeek-R1 needs "32 GPUs, each with 80 GiB", first-token latency 2.91 s, ~30 tokens/s.
- MeanCache: ~31% of queries repeat.
- Remaining Sec 4-6 content is search ranking (RankGPT, TourRank), robust RAG (ATM) and PA-RAG (the Writer's preference alignment), RLHB (user-behaviour alignment), quantization, pruning and speculative decoding. These surveys cite other papers' numbers.

LIMITS
- This is a blueprint and survey, not a controlled study. The authors say so: "Rather than focusing on a singular system and its evaluation" and "Instead of relying on statistics of performance metrics".
- There is no ablation of DAG vs ReAct vs a single agent, and no cost, latency or token comparison, despite the "reduced token consumption" claim. No planner failure rates, DAG sizes or re-plan frequency are given. No public benchmark is used.
- The evaluation compares the full system with Baidu's legacy search engine, so gains cannot be attributed to topology. The sample size is not given.
- The "single agent suffers task overload" argument in Sec 2 is asserted without evidence.
- Planner RL (GRPO rewards) and tool-doc refinement (DRAFT) are described but not evaluated here.
- The A/B result is modest (about 1-2%), and the human-eval gain exists only for complex queries.
- Dated: MCP is described as an HTTP+JSON-RPC protocol per the 2024-2025 intro. The inference section names DeepSeek-R1, LLaMA-4 and Qwen-3 as the large models.

BUILDS ON (as printed in the references)
- ReAct: Yao et al., ICLR 2023 (contrasted, not built on).
- RQ-RAG: Chan et al., arXiv 2404.00610, 2024 (contrasted).
- Rewrite-Retrieve-Read: Ma et al. 2023 (planner SFT data).
- MMOA-RAG: Chen et al. 2025b (joint multi-agent RL), using MAPPO from Yu et al., NeurIPS 2022.
- GRPO: Shao et al. 2024 (DeepSeekMath, arXiv 2402.03300).
- DRAFT (tool-doc refinement) and COLT (tool retrieval): Qu et al. 2025b and 2024 (Baidu/RUC group).
- TourRank: Chen et al., WWW 2025; RankGPT: Sun et al. 2023b.
- ATM (Zhu et al. 2024) and PA-RAG (Wu et al. 2024) for the Writer.
- MCP: Anthropic, Nov 2024.
- Also cited: HuggingGPT (Shen et al.), Toolformer (Schick et al.), k-means++ (Arthur and Vassilvitskii 2006), and DPO, PPO and Curriculum learning (Bengio 2009).
- The multi-agent decomposition itself is credited only to generic work ("Knuth 1997", "Cohen et al. 2007"). No prior multi-agent planner/executor system is named.

CODE: none in the paper. The only reusable formalism is the graph definition: the planner mapping "Φ: (q, T) → G" with vertex interface "⟨arg(v), ret(v)⟩" and tool binding "τ(v) ∈ T, or τ(v)=∅ for local LLM computation" (Sec 3.4, Eq. 10).

FIGURES (captions from the extracted text; the figures script was not run)
- Fig 1 (p.7), "The Overview of AI Search Paradigm". It is the best single candidate for the note: the Master picks a candidate team (Writer-Only, Executor-Inclusive, Planner-Enhanced), the Planner emits a DAG, the Executor runs it, the Writer answers, and the Master evaluates every stage and loops back to "Reflect, Re-Plan & Re-Act". It shows team selection plus the replan loop in one picture.
- Fig 2 (p.10), vanilla RAG vs ReAct/RQ-RAG vs the DAG paradigm. It is a secondary option.
- Fig 3 (p.12) is the capability boundary; the rest cover search ranking, RAG training and inference.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. The extraction is clean, apart from small math-symbol garbling in equations. References were skimmed, not read in full. Table 1 prints only the NWR column. The text says "relative enhancement of WTL by 13%", but the table metric is NWR, an inconsistent label in the source. I did not run the figures script, and the caption page numbers above come from the PDF's printed page numbers.
